evidence: Verg. G. 2.412–413: laudātō ingentia rūra, exiguum colitō
terms.comment: Bigger than magnus: Cicero remarks that the flatterer in Terence, asked whether Thais thanks his master “greatly”, answers not magnās but ingentīs (Cic. Lael. 98).

evidence: Caes. BG 6.16: simulācra immānī magnitūdine (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 3.70: ingēns immēnsusque campus (Lewis & Short)

terms.comment: Post-Augustan: first “out of rule, irregular” (from norma; Quint. 11.3.139), then “immense” (Tac., Plin., Suet.; Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: ‘magnās vērō agere grātiās Thāis mihi?’ satis erat respondēre ‘magnās’. ‘ingentīs’ inquit. semper auget assentātor id, quod is, cujus ad voluntātem dīcitur, volt esse magnum
phrases.english: ‘Is Thais really very grateful to me?’ It would have been enough to answer ‘very’; ‘hugely’, says he. The flatterer always makes bigger whatever the man he is pleasing wants to be big
praise huge estates; farm a small one

phrases.latin: ego stirpem ingentem, vestīgiō pedis ejus haerentem, revellī
phrases.english: I pulled out a huge thorn stuck in the sole of his paw

sources: Lewis & Short: ingens · Lewis & Short: immanis · Lewis & Short: immensus · Lewis & Short: enormis
